questions.question: Your gross pay is $500 and your income-tax deduction is $100. What is your net pay?
questions.explain: Net pay = gross pay minus deductions: $500 − $100 = $400. A common trap is adding the deduction instead of subtracting it.

questions.question: A lifeguard at a Vancouver pool earns $15 per hour and works 8 hours this week. What is the lifeguard's gross pay?
questions.explain: Gross pay = hourly rate × hours = $15 × 8 = $120. Miscounting the hours (7 or 9) gives the nearby wrong answers.

questions.question: Which of the following is a deduction taken from gross pay to arrive at net pay?
questions.explain: Income tax is subtracted from gross pay. Commission is a type of income (added to gross), and gross/net pay are amounts, not deductions.

questions.question: A graphic designer in Kelowna earns a salary of $40,000 per year. Total yearly deductions are $8,000. What is the designer's net pay?
questions.explain: Net pay = gross − deductions = $40,000 − $8,000 = $32,000. The trap is accidentally adding the deduction or reading the deduction amount as the answer.

questions.question: A barista in Surrey earns $20 per hour and works 35 hours. Her pay stub shows 12 % withheld for income tax and a flat $30 benefits premium. What is her net pay for the period?
questions.explain: Gross = $700; tax = 0.12 × $700 = $84; net = $700 − $84 − $30 = $586. The most common error is dropping one of the two deductions, giving $616 or $670.

questions.question: A car salesperson in Abbotsford earns a base salary of $3,000 per month plus a 5 % commission on total sales. If this month's sales are $12,000, what is her gross pay?
questions.explain: Gross = base + commission = $3,000 + (0.05 × $12,000) = $3,000 + $600 = $3,600. A frequent slip is misplacing the decimal so 5 % of $12,000 becomes $60 instead of $600.

questions.question: A Grade-12 student earns $14 per hour for 20 hours. The pay stub deducts 10 % for income tax and $20 for CPP. What is the student's net pay?
questions.explain: Gross = $280; tax = $28; net = $280 − $28 − $20 = $232. Forgetting one deduction (giving $252 or $260) or misreading the CPP figure (giving $202) are the usual traps.

questions.question: Person A earns $20 per hour × 25 hours with 10 % tax withheld. Person B earns a flat $480 per pay period with $30 in deductions. Who has the higher net pay?
options: They earn the same net pay
questions.explain: A: $500 − $50 = $450. B: $480 − $30 = $450. They match exactly. The trap is skipping A's tax and thinking A nets $500, or miscalculating one of the two amounts.

questions.question: A construction worker in BC earns $20 per hour × 30 hours. The pay stub lists three percentage deductions: 10 % income tax, 5 % CPP, and 2 % EI, all calculated on gross pay. What is the worker's net pay?
questions.explain: Gross = $600. Deductions: $60 + $30 + $12 = $102. Net = $600 − $102 = $498. The common error is computing only one or two of the three percentages, yielding $540 (tax only) or $510 (tax + CPP).

questions.question: A part-time tutor's gross pay is $40 per hour × 20 hours = $800. Deductions are 15 % income tax and a $40 insurance premium. What is the tutor's effective net hourly rate (total net pay divided by hours worked)?
questions.explain: Net = $800 − $120 − $40 = $640; effective rate = $640 ÷ 20 = $32/hr. The big trap is answering $40 (the gross rate) or $34 (forgetting the $40 insurance premium).

questions.question: A real-estate agent in Burnaby earns a 10 % commission on all sales. In May sales were $20,000; in June they were $25,000. Each month, 20 % of gross pay is withheld as tax and a flat $50 is deducted for CPP. How much MORE net pay did the agent earn in June than in May?
questions.explain: Extra gross = $500; extra tax = 20 % × $500 = $100; CPP is the same both months, so extra net = $500 − $100 = $400. The trap is answering $500 by ignoring the tax on the additional income.

questions.question: A software tester in Victoria earns $20/hr × 30 hours and receives a $100 performance bonus in the same pay period. All percentage deductions (10 % tax, 5 % CPP, 1 % EI) are calculated on total gross pay. What is net pay?
questions.explain: The bonus is part of gross, so every percentage applies to $700 (not just $600). Deductions = $70 + $35 + $7 = $112; net = $700 − $112 = $588. The key misconception is computing deductions only on the regular wage and adding the bonus tax-free, giving $604.
